title: 2.1.8 Chain Three Branches
description: Write an else if chain with at least three branches. Auto-graded.
sourceRef: designed: practice for 'Several Conditions: else if', book 2.1.4

steps.title: Declare a battery level
steps.instructions: Create a variable called batteryPercent and set it to a number from 0 to 100.

steps.title: Chain at least three branches
steps.instructions: Write an if / else if / else if / else chain that logs a status: below 20 logs 'Low battery', below 50 logs 'Battery ok', below 90 logs 'Battery good', and anything else logs 'Battery full'. This chain uses < comparisons, not >=, so check the lowest cutoff first -- the opposite order from the grade example, which uses >= and checks the highest cutoff first.

planChart.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[set batteryPercent from 0 to 100]
  B --> C{below 20}
  C -- yes --> D[/log Low battery/]
  C -- no --> E{below 50}
  E -- yes --> F[/log Battery ok/]
  E -- no --> G{below 90}
  G -- yes --> H[/log Battery good/]
  G -- no --> I[/log Battery full/]
  D --> J([End])
  F --> J
  H --> J
  I --> J

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote JavaScript for the lab "2.1.8 Chain Three Branches". The task they were given: Create a variable called batteryPercent and set it to a number from 0 to 100. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, template strings, arrow functions, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment never runs. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.
